angle: The fluid dynamics angle: concentration-discharge behavior, dilution mass balance, and modeled streamflow
verdict: PURSUE NARROWLY, AND NOT AS A DISCHARGE ANGLE. The specific hypothesis this angle was commissioned to test - that knowing discharge at an ungauged site converts into BETWEEN-SITE skill for nitrate concentration and 10 mg/L exceedance, via a dilution mass balance C = load/Q or C ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge - is not supported by any verified evidence, and is contradicted by the sign of the C-Q relation. Nitrate in this region is MOBILIZING/ENRICHING (C-Q exponent b > 0), not diluting: on this project's own 20 usable gauged sites a verifier measured median b = +0.61, and a recomputation of the Marinos et al. UMRB archive found b > 0 at 32 of 32 sites (median +0.44). A dilution denominator is therefore the wrong functional form. Three independent lines then close the between-site question specifically: (a) Basu et al. 2010 propose the flow-weighted-concentration decomposition C_f = L_T/Q_T that motivates this whole angle, but NEVER fit or report any between-site regression of C_f on N inputs, land use, or specific discharge - the framework exists, the evidence does not; (b) an unverified recomputation of the Marinos archive with PERFECT measured co-located discharge found log10(mean specific discharge) explains R2 = 0.034 of between-site mean nitrate and adds delta-R2 = +0.001 on top of row-crop + tile (n=32); (c) an unverified 759-catchment German study computed the full hydrological-descriptor suite (mean Q, mean specific Q, runoff coefficient, baseflow index, flashiness) and found it improved TOC models by 11-37% while NOT surfacing a single hydrological descriptor in the top six of ANY of its four nitrate models. Since (b) is measured with real gauged Q, modeled Q (NWM) can only be worse - it adds error on top of a between-site signal that is already near zero. It must be stated plainly that this is a DIFFERENT failure from the project's prior one: advective in-channel travel-time routing was already implemented and already failed as part of the 'lagged weather hurt' result (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019); the mass-balance side was genuinely untested, and this synthesis is the first assessment of it. The two are independent, and the mass-balance side fails for its own reason - not timing mis-specification, but the absence of a between-site level relation between flow and concentration. WHAT IS WORTH TAKING FROM THIS ANGLE: the C-Q literature's own answer to 'what sets a site's absolute level' is the power-law INTERCEPT, not the slope, and the intercept is controlled by static land-use and subsurface attributes - above all TILE DRAINAGE DENSITY. This angle's highest-value output is therefore a correction to the project brief: the brief states tile drainage has 'NO data source identified yet', and that is false. Two free, CONUS/Midwest-wide, static, ungauged-compatible tile rasters exist (AgTile-US, verified; Nakagaki & Wieczorek USGS, unverified), and they are exactly the static-geography feature class that has produced every win on this project. Secondarily, IF NWM is touched at all, it should supply STATIC per-basin flow signatures (mean specific discharge, baseflow index, flashiness, runoff ratio) targeting the between-site term, never per-day discharge - and only after a cheap pre-test against the 22 gauged sites. Expected value of the NWM path is LOW; expected value of the tile-drainage path extracted from this angle is HIGH.

findings.claim: The dilution framing is the WRONG SIGN for agricultural nitrate in this region. On this project's OWN data, a verifier computed per-site log-log C-Q fits at the 20 usable gauged sites and found median power-law exponent b = +0.61 - strongly mobilizing/enriching, not diluting (dilution requires b < 0; chemostasis is b ~ 0). A recomputation of the Marinos et al. (2020) UMRB archive found b > 0 at 32 of 32 sites, range +0.090 to +1.095, median +0.440; not a single site diluted on the daily-mean timescale (that recomputation is UNVERIFIED and is cited here only as corroboration, not as warrant). Consequence: a feature or target of the form C = load / Q, or any specific-discharge dilution denominator, encodes a relationship whose sign is opposite to the observed physics. Any gain from such a feature would come from XGBoost inverting it, not from the mass balance being right.
findings.effectSize: project's own gauged sites: median C-Q exponent b = +0.61 (verifier recomputation, n=20 sites). Corroborating unverified UMRB recomputation: b>0 at 32/32 sites, median +0.44, range +0.090 to +1.095

findings.claim: The between-site relation this angle was built on WAS NEVER ESTIMATED IN THE SOURCE LITERATURE. Basu et al. (2010, GRL, DOI 10.1029/2010GL045168) is the canonical citation for 'concentration = load / discharge as a stable per-catchment constant', and it does propose the flow-weighted concentration C_f = L_T/Q_T as an index of 'effective biogeochemical stationarity', asserting that 'the anthropogenic drivers (e.g., land-use; nutrient inputs) are reflected in C_f'. But the paper NEVER fits that relation: there is no regression of C_f on N input, N surplus, land use, or specific discharge, and NO between-catchment R2 appears anywhere in it. C_f is obtained as a per-catchment fitted slope from that catchment's OWN observed loads, which requires local nitrate observations. Anyone citing Basu 2010 as evidence that C ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge is a validated between-site predictor is over-reading a decomposition framework as an empirical result.
findings.effectSize: Zero between-site R2 reported. The paper's only headline R2 (0.7 +/- 0.2) is a WITHIN-catchment inter-annual regression of annual load on annual discharge, fit separately per catchment, with Q on both sides of the equation.
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable (in-sample OLS on annual aggregates, per catchment; no spatial, temporal, or random holdout)

findings.claim: MEASURED specific discharge is near-worthless as a between-site predictor of nitrate level, which bounds modeled discharge from above. UNVERIFIED (recomputed by a researcher from the Marinos et al. 2020 public HydroShare archive, n=32 UMRB sites with perfect co-located USGS discharge): log10(mean specific discharge) explains R2 = 0.034 of between-site mean nitrate and R2 = 0.097 of between-site fraction-of-days >= 10 mg/L; added to a %row-crop + %tile model it moves R2 from 0.486 to 0.487 (delta = +0.001). By contrast %agriculture alone gives R2 = 0.539 and %forest alone R2 = 0.550 for the same response. THIS FINDING IS UNVERIFIED and must not be treated as the warrant for a decision on its own - but its logic is decisive if it holds, because a modeled discharge source (NWM, SPARROW) can only add error on top of a signal that is already near zero. It is also consistent with, and its direction is independently supported by, the verified fact that Basu et al. never found such a relation to report.

findings.claim: In the largest between-site nitrate study in this evidence set, discharge-derived descriptors helped organic carbon but NOT nitrate. UNVERIFIED (Ebeling et al. 2021, DOI 10.1029/2020WR028134): the study computed mean discharge, mean SPECIFIC discharge, runoff coefficient, seasonal ratio, base-flow index and flashiness index for a 184-catchment subset. These raised TOC model skill 'between 11% and 37%' (RF slope-b R2_crossval 0.28 -> 0.44). For NITRATE, no improvement is reported anywhere, and not one hydrological descriptor appears in the top six of ANY of the four NO3-N models; those are topped instead by land cover, precipitation climatology, subsurface/aquifer type, slope and TWI. This is the closest thing in the corpus to a direct answer to the research question, and it answers it negatively - but it is UNVERIFIED, and absence-of-reporting is weaker than an explicit stated null. Note also these are OBSERVED gauge discharges, so this does not separately test modeled-Q bias, and the study contains no tile-drainage predictor at all ('drain_dens' there is stream drainage density, not artificial subsurface drainage).
findings.effectSize: hydrological descriptors: +11% to +37% explained variance for TOC; no reported gain for NO3-N; zero hydrological descriptors in the top-6 of any of the four NO3-N models

findings.claim: Even a PERFECT discharge series at an ungauged pin would explain only a minority of within-site nitrate variance, and that variance is the timing term this project already handles. UNVERIFIED (Ebeling et al. 2021, plus a researcher's recomputation from the paper's own CC-BY WQQDB dataset): across 274-275 German catchments the log-log C-Q power-law regression for NO3-N had mean R2 = 0.27 +/- 0.24, recomputed median R2 = 0.223 (quartiles 0.044 / 0.223 / 0.458), with only 39.4% of catchments exceeding R2 = 0.30. A VERIFIED parallel exists on this project's own data: at the 20 usable gauged sites, log Q explains a MEDIAN 50.9% of the variance in log nitrate concentration (per-site R2 range 0.21-0.87). The two figures differ by region and by data density, but agree on the structural point that matters here: this is a WITHIN-SITE, non-spatially-held-out diagnostic. It speaks to within_r2 = 0.42 - the timing term the model already does well - and says nothing about between_r2 = 0.21, where essentially all remaining headroom sits.

findings.claim: THE LOAD-AS-TARGET PROPOSAL IS A TRAP, ON THE SOURCE LITERATURE'S OWN ADMISSION. Basu et al. (2010) state that linear fits to the annual load-discharge relation 'are judged adequate (R2>0.8) for a range of b values (-0.4 < b < 1.4)' - a band wide enough to include strong dilution AND strong mobilization - and explicitly acknowledge the standing critique that the L-Q correlation 'is a spurious correlation since discharge is a component of load calculation'. Switching the modeling target from concentration to load (C x Q) would therefore manufacture a high R2 that is largely an artifact of Q appearing on both sides, and back-deriving concentration as L/Q would recover none of the between-site concentration skill. This is compounded by the enrichment finding above: since b > 0 essentially everywhere, load scales as roughly Q^(1+b) with 1+b in the range 1.09-2.10, so a load target is MORE dominated by discharge than a concentration target, and back-dividing by a MODELED Q would propagate NWM discharge error directly into the recovered concentration. Changing the target definition is not a route to between-site skill.
findings.effectSize: linear L-Q fits reach R2 > 0.8 across the whole range -0.4 < b < 1.4, i.e. R2 > 0.8 is attained even for strongly non-chemostatic C-Q behavior. Load exponent 1+b in range 1.09-2.10 (from the unverified UMRB recomputation).

findings.claim: THE CHEMOSTASIS PREMISE THAT MOTIVATED THIS ANGLE'S 'KILL SWITCH' IS ITSELF WRONG, AND THE PROPOSED CHEAP TEST HAS A BROKEN DECISION RULE. The plan was: compute CVc/CVq on the 22 gauged sites; if the median is well below 1, declare nitrate chemostatic and abandon the fluid-dynamics angle. A verifier RAN this test: median CVc/CVq = 0.443 on the 20 usable gauged sites - 'well below 1', which by the stated criterion would kill the angle. Yet at those same sites log Q explains a median 50.9% of log-nitrate variance with median b = +0.61. CVc/CVq is low there because CVq is LARGE (median 1.4), not because C is insensitive to Q. CVc/CVq is a variance ratio, not a mutual-information measure; it conflates 'C is buffered' with 'Q is wild'. Three further corrections: (a) the widely quoted '< 0.3 chemostatic threshold' is NOT a community standard - it is 0.17 + 2 SD of GEOGENIC solutes at Thompson et al.'s own 31 subwatersheds; the thresholds actually used in the literature are 0.5 (following Thompson et al. 2011) or 1.0 (Musolff et al. 2015), and the attribution should be to Thompson et al. 2011 AND Musolff et al. 2015; (b) Thompson et al.'s own nitrate result is mean CVc/CVq = 0.70 (SD 0.49) - above any chemostatic line for most sites, in a paper with only 2 agricultural catchments; (c) Basu et al. 2010 state plainly that nutrient export in the MARB is NON-chemostatic at the DAILY and MONTHLY timescales, and chemostasis emerges only after annual aggregation - so the chemostatic result offers no support at this project's operative timescale (daily-max concentration, daily 10 mg/L flag) and no support at this project's basin sizes. The angle must not be killed on a chemostasis argument; it should be killed, if at all, on the absence of a between-site Q-to-level relation.
findings.effectSize: project's own gauged sites: median CVc/CVq = 0.443 with median CVq = 1.4, alongside median within-site C-Q R2 = 0.509 and b = +0.61. Thompson et al. 2011 nitrate: mean CVc/CVq = 0.70 (SD 0.49). Literature thresholds: 0.5 or 1.0, NOT 0.3.

findings.claim: WHAT THE C-Q LITERATURE SAYS ACTUALLY SETS A SITE'S ABSOLUTE LEVEL IS THE POWER-LAW INTERCEPT, AND THE INTERCEPT IS CONTROLLED BY STATIC LAND USE AND TILE DRAINAGE - NOT BY FLOW. Verified: Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020) report for the Upper Mississippi River Basin that 'tile drainage is a dominant control on C-Q dynamics, with increasing drainage density contributing to more chemostatic C-Q behavior', and that concentration variability rises relative to discharge variability with increasing basin size across SIX orders of magnitude. UNVERIFIED corroboration from a recomputation of that paper's archive (n=32) makes the level/dynamics separation explicit: the fitted power-law intercept log10(a) - the site's absolute level after removing flow - is land-use controlled (%agriculture R2 = 0.585, %forest R2 = 0.649, %row crop R2 = 0.513, %tile R2 = 0.251) but barely scale controlled (log10(area) R2 = 0.179); conversely CVc/CVq is a scale property (log10(area) R2 = 0.412) and essentially unrelated to land use (%tile R2 = 0.001). The same unverified recomputation reports that % subsurface tile drainage ALONE explains R2 = 0.575 of the between-site variance in FRACTION OF DAYS WITH NITRATE >= 10 mg/L - literally this project's classification target and literally its weakest term (between_rate_r2 = 0.24) - versus %agriculture 0.502, %row crop 0.488, %forest 0.441, log10(area) 0.252. All of those figures are UNVERIFIED, in-sample cross-sectional fits with no holdout, and are NOT comparable to LOFO 0.820; they are evidence about which covariate class carries between-site information, not an expected effect size.
findings.effectSize: VERIFIED: direction only - increasing tile drainage density -> more chemostatic; CVc/CVq rises with basin size across six orders of magnitude. findings.claim: THE PROJECT BRIEF CONTAINS A CORRECTABLE FACTUAL ERROR, AND FIXING IT IS THIS ANGLE'S HIGHEST-VALUE OUTPUT. The brief states tile drainage density is 'known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet.' A free, CONUS-wide, static, unauthenticated data source exists: AgTile-US (Valayamkunnath et al. 2020, Scientific Data 7:257, DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x), 30 m binary tile-drained cropland, validated at 86.03% CONUS-wide against 16,000 ground-truth points and 91.1% in IOWA specifically on 5,253 points, with the heavily tile-drained Midwest spanning 82.7-93.6%. A second, independent option is the Nakagaki & Wieczorek USGS 12-state layer, which stores CONTINUOUS tile-drained area per cell rather than a binary flag (UNVERIFIED). CRITICAL METRIC CORRECTION, applied from verification: '86.03% accuracy' is NOT balanced two-class accuracy - the paper pairs it with '13.97% omission error' summing to exactly 100%, because ALL 16,000 ground-truth points are known-DRAINED locations photo-interpreted from tile signatures on fallow cropland. It is producer's accuracy / recall on positives only. No confusion matrix, no true negatives, no commission error, no kappa is reported anywhere. This matters directly: a basin-MEAN tile fraction is biased precisely by commission error, the one error mode never measured. Describe it as '86.03% of known tile-drained ground-truth points correctly captured (omission error only; commission error unquantified)'.

findings.claim: MANDATORY REDUNDANCY CAVEAT ON THE TILE FEATURE: AgTile-US is a deterministic reallocation of county census totals, not an observation. For each county the decision tree selects cells starting from the most poorly drained SSURGO class at zero slope, incrementing slope and stepping down drainage class until accumulated area matches the county's 2017 USDA census tile acreage; the cropland mask is NLCD 2016. Therefore county aggregates reproduce the census BY CONSTRUCTION (Iowa modeled 5,706,831 ha vs census 5,708,945 ha = -0.04%, which is a calibration target and NOT independent skill), the map's genuine added value is sub-county allocation driven only by gSSURGO drainage class and slope, and its errors are spatially structured by county boundary with step discontinuities there. Effective independent information is roughly county-scale (99 counties in Iowa), not 30 m. Two error sources are quantified by the authors: USDA census tile estimates carry ~19.8% average error, and NLCD 2016 underestimates cropland by -18.15% nationally, so tile fraction is biased LOW and unevenly. THE REAL RISK: tile fraction is spatially very smooth across Iowa (Des Moines Lobe vs Loess Hills / driftless southeast) and lon and lat are already the #2 and #3 permutation-importance features - XGBoost may have already absorbed most of this signal through coordinates. Run the ablation against a lat/lon-INCLUDED baseline, and read a null result as 'already captured by coordinates', not as 'tile drainage does not matter'. A control arm aggregating gSSURGO drainage class and slope directly would separate the two.
findings.effectSize: Iowa county-total agreement -0.04% (by construction). USDA census average error 19.8%; NLCD 2016 cropland underestimate -18.15% nationally. At n=19 LOFO folds, a ~20% multiplicative noise floor on the covariate caps achievable between-site gain.

findings.claim: NWM CONTAINS NO TILE-DRAINAGE REPRESENTATION AT ALL, VERIFIED THROUGH v3.1 - but the derived 'systematic low bias scaling with tile density' inference is NOT supported and should be dropped. Verified quote from Valayamkunnath et al. 2022 (WRR 58(4), DOI 10.1029/2021WR031242): 'The current NWM lacks TD representation which adds considerable uncertainty to streamflow forecasts in heavily tile-drained areas.' Independently verified by source inspection of NCAR/wrf_hydro_nwm_public v5.4.0 (March 2025, consistent with operational NWM v3.1): no tile-drainage module, no OPT_TDRN or TILE_DRAIN/TDRAIN namelist option, nothing in docs/userguide/model-physics.rest - only generic Noah-MP QDRAIN bottom drainage. The omission persists through v3.1. THREE CORRECTIONS TO HOW THIS WAS BEING USED: (1) The study is NWM V2.0, 49 calibration basins (tile area >= 10%, 10-20,000 km2) from a 188-gauge pool, 139 gauges for regional evaluation, and the split is TEMPORAL on the SAME basins (calibrate WY2008-2013, evaluate Oct 2013 - Oct 2019), NOT leave-one-basin-out. Its Gower's-distance regionalization from 49 donors to 939 HUC10 receivers is never independently validated, so this paper provides NO evidence about ungauged transfer. (2) The +14% peak / +2.3% volume / +11% baseflow figures are MODEL-MINUS-MODEL sensitivities (TD-on vs TD-off within a calibrated parameter set), not measured biases against observations. Adding TD without recalibration barely moves the level at all ('There are no considerable differences in the estimated Bias between Default and DefaultTD'); what TD buys is DYNAMICS and TIMING (COR +0.15, NSE +0.16, KGE +0.22 for high flows; event hit rate 44% -> ~65%; false-alarm 22.5% -> 17.5%). (3) The bias SIGN is wrong in the original inference: in the calibrated configuration the paper reports median event peak-flow bias +5% (HIGH, not low), reduced to +0.57% with TD, and low flows OVERESTIMATED (CalibTD still +50%). The -43% to -50% figure is GROUNDWATER RECHARGE, an internal flux absent from the streamflow product. Most decisively, the paper NEVER regresses bias against tile-drainage percentage, and its design cannot: both gauge sets are pre-screened to tile fraction >= 10%, truncating the range of the exact covariate the inference needs.

TD scheme recovers 20-50% of the uncalibrated-to-calibrated gap (a median-of-seasonal-distributions statement on the 49 calibration basins).

findings.claim: MOST IMPORTANT REFRAMING OF THE NWM PROPOSITION: everything the tile-drainage study demonstrates NWM currently gets WRONG - timing, peak shape, event hit rate, flashiness - is the axis on which this model is ALREADY strong ('a good timer', within_r2 0.42), while the LEVEL effect is largely absorbed by calibration. The prior expectation that NWM discharge will fix the between-site LEVEL deficit should therefore be LOW on the paper's own evidence. Combined with the corrected Towler benchmark (below) and the near-zero between-site R2 of even PERFECT specific discharge, the ordering is clear: NWM Q is a plausible within-site timing covariate for a model that does not need one, and a poor between-site level covariate for a model that desperately needs one. NWM v3.0 also has no explicit tile-drainage representation, so it does not supply the known-missing Iowa control either.

findings.claim: NWM v2.1 SKILL AT GAUGED SITES IS MODEST AND THE HEADLINE NUMBERS ARE PARTLY IN-SAMPLE - with a correction that cuts AGAINST the pessimistic reading for Iowa specifically. Towler et al. 2023 (HESS 27:1809-1834, DOI 10.5194/hess-27-1809-2023) evaluated NWM v2.1 and NHM v1.0 daily streamflow against 5,390 USGS gauges over 1 Oct 1983 - 31 Dec 2016. CORRECTED VALUES: the Central region (n = 1,450, an aggregation of Falcone 2011 ecoregions - NOT HUC2) had median KGE 0.45 for NWMv2.1 and 0.33 for NHMv1.0, NOT the 0.40 / 0.29 originally claimed (0.29 is the West/NHM value). Regional medians (NHM/NWM): West 0.29/0.32, Central 0.33/0.45, Southeast 0.48/0.56, Northeast 0.63/0.65; CONUS-wide NWMv2.1 median 0.53. Central NWMv2.1 also shows r = 0.71, rSD = 0.87, PBIAS = +4.4%. THE PROTOCOL IS NOT A TEMPORAL HOLDOUT: both models' calibration periods overlap the evaluation window (NWMv2.1 calibrated WY2008-2013 at 1,378 predominantly natural-flow gauged basins with parameters regionalized elsewhere by hydrologic similarity), and the authors flag the resulting bias explicitly - so 0.45 is optimistic. TWO CORRECTIONS THAT CUT AGAINST THE ORIGINAL PESSIMISM: (a) the 'poor plains performance' sentence names North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas and Texas - all WEST of Iowa; Iowa sits in the eastern portion the paper calls 'more mixed' (not 'most mixed', a misquote), so this quote must NOT be used to imply NWM is specifically poor over Iowa, and no HUC-07 figure exists in the paper. (b) The Central KGE shortfall is driven mainly by correlation (r 0.71) and variability ratio (rSD 0.87) rather than volume bias (PBIAS +4.4%) - i.e. it is a TIMING/VARIABILITY deficit, on the axis where this project is already adequate, not the between-site level term where the headroom lies.

findings.claim: MODELED-Q BIAS IN IOWA MAY BE SPATIALLY STRUCTURED EAST-WEST, WHICH WOULD BE THE WORST POSSIBLE FAILURE MODE HERE. UNVERIFIED (Zhang et al. / Water 15:2319, DOI 10.3390/w15132319): Iowa is split between two River Forecast Centers, and per-RFC median percent bias diverges in sign. North Central RFC (humid, eastern/Mississippi-draining Iowa, 55 natural-flow + 362 regulated gauges) natural-flow median PBIAS -10.15% (Q1 -20.21, Q3 +2.19) for 100-500 km2 basins and -3.08% for >500 km2 - systematic UNDER-estimation, worst at the smaller sizes that dominate this project's sites. Missouri Basin RFC (western Iowa, 58 NF + 269 RF) natural-flow median PBIAS +4.46% / +5.93% / +11.02% by increasing basin size - systematic OVER-estimation. That is a swing of order 15-20 percentage points across the state. Since lon and lat are already the #2 and #3 features by permutation importance, a west-east modeled-Q artifact would inject a spurious gradient into exactly the covariates the model leans on hardest. Also unverified from the same source: NCRFC regulated-flow median PBIAS is +47.14% at 10-100 km2 basins (vs +0.99% at 100-500 km2) - and small headwater basins are where an arbitrary map pin is most likely to land; and NWM is weakest in SPRING in humid regions ('the model tends to underestimate streamflow during the spring season'), precisely the April-June flush window when Iowa nitrate violations concentrate. ALL OF THIS IS UNVERIFIED and must not be the sole warrant for a decision - but it is cheap to check directly and should be checked before any NWM ingestion.

findings.claim: THE CHEAPEST DECISIVE EXPERIMENT DOMINATES FURTHER LITERATURE SEARCH ON THIS ANGLE, AND USES ONLY DATA ALREADY ON DISK PLUS ONE FREE DOWNLOAD. Pull NWM v3.0 retrospective Q by COMID (the join is verified; the comids are already stored per basin) at the 22 USGS-gauged sites, and (a) compute per-site KGE and MONTHLY PBIAS against observed Q, paying particular attention to April-June; (b) regress NWM-vs-observed percent bias on AgTile-US tile fraction across those 22 sites; (c) test whether NWM Q at those sites carries any marginal information beyond the weather and basin-geometry features already in the model, since NWM Q is itself largely a deterministic function of the same inputs. This measures the error structure directly in Iowa instead of inferring it from CONUS-scale benchmarks, needs no new data acquisition beyond one figshare download, and settles in days what the literature cannot settle at all. RUN THE ACCESS-COST CHECK FIRST (UNVERIFIED but cheap and directly measured by a researcher): chrtout Zarr arrays are chunked [672 time, 30000 feature_id] at 3.94 MB per compressed streamflow chunk, requiring 573 time-chunks per feature-chunk for the full record - so extraction cost is ~573 x (distinct feature-chunks touched) x 3.94 MB, best case ~2 GB if all 85 site COMIDs fall in one 30,000-reach chunk, worst case ~190 GB if they land in 85 separate chunks. Download the 22 MB feature_id coordinate array, compute floor(index/30000) for the project's COMIDs, and count distinct values. That decides in minutes whether this is a coffee-break job or a multi-day transfer.

findings.claim: A GENUINELY UNTESTED MASS-BALANCE PRESCRIPTION SURVIVES, IN A DIFFERENT FORM THAN PROPOSED - AND IT IS DEPLOYMENT-COMPATIBLE. Under the Basu formulation the invariant quantity is the flow-weighted concentration C_f = L_T/Q_T, a RATIO. So the mass balance predicts site-mean concentration ~ (delivered N load per unit area) / (long-term mean annual runoff depth): the hydrologic term does not drop out, it moves into the DENOMINATOR as a long-term water-yield NORMALIZER. That is a materially different engineering prescription from either 'use raw N surplus and row-crop fraction' (what the model does now) or 'add daily discharge' (what this angle proposed). The concrete feature is a static per-basin ratio, (N surplus or row-crop fraction) / (long-term mean annual runoff or precipitation), computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin from climatological normals with no discharge record and no local history. IMPORTANT HONESTY CONSTRAINT: no verified source reports an R2 for this relation. Basu et al. explicitly never fit it. It is a theoretically motivated, cheap, static, deployment-compatible candidate - not a validated one - and the unverified evidence that specific discharge alone carries R2 = 0.034 between sites should temper expectations for the denominator's contribution. Its cost is 1-2 static columns against ~19 effective units, which is affordable; test it against a baseline that already includes the raw unnormalized source terms so the normalization is what is being evaluated.

findings.claim: A CO-EQUAL FINDING FROM THE LSTM LITERATURE POINTS AT THE TRANSFERABLE HALF: static SOIL and PHYSIOGRAPHIC attributes rank alongside discharge as the strongest influences on nitrate model performance. UNVERIFIED (Gorski et al. 2024, WRR, DOI 10.1029/2023WR036591): across 46 predominantly agricultural midwestern and eastern US sites, 'discharge and watershed soil and physiographic attributes showed a strong influence on model performance', ranked above nitrogen-application, land-use and climate attributes. CRITICAL PROTOCOL QUALIFICATION: the discharge used was daily OBSERVED discharge at gauged, intensively monitored sites, and every one of the four modeling schemes trained on data FROM the sites being predicted - there is no experiment in which a site is entirely withheld. So its headline median KGE 0.66 (46 single-site models) is a WITHIN-SITE temporal metric, NOT comparable to this project's LOFO 0.820 AUC or between_r2 0.21, and it provides ZERO evidence that a modeled-Q surrogate retains that information or that the discharge signal transfers to an unmonitored site. The transferable half is the SOIL and PHYSIOGRAPHIC half - a feature class this project entirely lacks (no soil, no drainage class, no depth-to-water-table, no slope, no relief; static geography is carried by lat, lon, log_basin_area alone). The paper's full data and code are released free and public-domain by USGS at DOI 10.5066/P1N6P2QL, supplying a ready-made static attribute list already assembled for 46 US agricultural basins, several in Iowa.

findings.claim: A RELEVANT NEGATIVE RESULT THAT CUTS BOTH WAYS ON THE n=19 CONSTRAINT. UNVERIFIED (Gorski et al. 2024): pooling all 46 sites into one global LSTM did NOT beat site-specific or grouped models - median KGE 0.63 (global) vs 0.66 (single-site) vs 0.66 (5 clusters by basin attributes) vs 0.65 with RMSE 1.03 mg/L (8 models grouped by glacial hydrogeologic terrane). The authors conclude there is 'a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model', explicitly contrasting water quality with the streamflow-LSTM literature where global training wins, and note 'it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents'. This falsifies naive transfer of the CAMELS 'more basins always help' finding to nitrate. IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: it weakens the argument that n=19 families is fatal, AND weakens the argument that acquiring more sites would fix the between-site deficit. A secondary and more actionable point: hydrogeologic-TERRANE grouping performed on par with attribute clustering, suggesting an explicit glacial-landform / terrane encoding (Des Moines Lobe vs Iowan Surface vs Southern Iron Clay vs Loess Hills) as a candidate replacement for the raw lat/lon features that currently rank #2 and #3 - if terrane encoding beats lat/lon, the between-site deficit is a missing-geology problem; if it does not, lat/lon is capturing something else. CAVEAT: 5-8 groups over 46 sites is ~6-9 sites per group; at 19 families the equivalent gives ~2-4 families per group, likely below the point where a group-specific model can be fit at all - so use terrane as a FEATURE, not as a model-partitioning scheme.

findings.claim: CHEMOSTASIS IS NOT A SAFE MODELING PRIOR FOR IOWA ROW-CROP BASINS, AND ITS BREAKDOWN IS ITSELF INFORMATIVE ABOUT THE BETWEEN-SITE PROBLEM. UNVERIFIED (Ebeling et al. 2021, n=274-759 German catchments): among agriculturally dominated catchments (f_agric >= 0.5), 34% exhibited CHEMODYNAMIC export regimes - 89% of those combined with enrichment - versus only 17% among less-agricultural catchments. Higher agricultural fraction was associated with HIGHER slope b and HIGHER CVc/CVq, the opposite of the homogenization expectation. The authors state directly: 'Our study therefore does not support the generality of the hypothesis that highly managed, agricultural catchments are necessarily subject to homogenization of sources and thus to chemostatic export regimes (Basu et al., 2010; Thompson et al., 2011).' They attribute the chemodynamic behaviour to vertical concentration heterogeneity from subsurface denitrification producing a depth decline in nitrate - high flow taps shallow, N-rich water. THREE CONSEQUENCES: (a) do not assume a fixed chemostatic C-Q form as a modeling prior; (b) mean nitrate AND ITS VARIANCE AMONG SITES both increase with agricultural land use, so the highest-agriculture Iowa basins are precisely the hardest to place on an absolute level - which is exactly the reported failure mode (between_r2 0.21); (c) the mechanism identified is a STATIC subsurface redox attribute, obtainable without any local sensor, and ranked first in 3 of 4 dynamics models - a candidate feature class this project has not tried. This is UNVERIFIED and where it bears on the C-Q regime it agrees with the verified Iowa-region evidence (b > 0, enrichment), so no conflict arises.

findings.claim: IMPORTANT NEGATIVE ON N-SURPLUS PRODUCTS THAT CORROBORATES ONE OF THIS PROJECT'S OWN FAILURES. UNVERIFIED (Ebeling et al. 2021, n=759): nitrogen surplus was a WEAKER between-site predictor of mean nitrate than plain land-cover fraction. Forest fraction alone explained 32% and agricultural fraction alone 29% of between-catchment variance in mean NO3-N, while the correlation of mean NO3-N with N_surp_80 (1980-2015 legacy-inclusive surplus) was only r = 0.39, i.e. r2 ~ 0.15 - despite N surplus correlating strongly with agricultural land (r = 0.71). N surplus does NOT appear in the top six predictors in either the PLSR or the RF model. Separately, VERIFIED (Basu et al. 2010): annual flow-weighted concentration in the MARB stayed temporally invariant DESPITE an approximately 1.5-fold increase in nutrient inputs over three decades, and Baltic efforts to cut inputs ~50% 'have failed to show positive results'; export is 'transport- rather than supply-limited, such that contemporary distributed and point sources have lesser influence.' TOGETHER these say the gTREND N-surplus product may be the WRONG VARIABLE, not merely the wrong vintage - which independently explains this project's -0.166 result from broadcasting 2017 surplus forward, and predicts that a time-invariant per-basin legacy-N or long-term-mean-surplus parameterization is strictly better than a time-varying one. Practical read: crop/land-cover fractions plus subsurface and tile attributes beat an N-budget product.
findings.effectSize: UNVERIFIED: f_forest alone R2 = 0.32, f_agric alone R2 = 0.29, N_surp_80 r = 0.39 (r2 ~ 0.15), N surplus absent from top-6 of both models. VERIFIED: ~1.5x input increase over three decades with no change in annual flow-weighted concentration; ~50% Baltic reduction target produced no detected improvement.
findings.splitProtocol: Ebeling: random-fold whole-catchment CV (not spatially blocked, optimistic). Basu: not-applicable, long-term observational trend description.
findings.nBasins: 759 German catchments (unverified); 21 MARB + 14 BSDB (verified)
sources: Ebeling et al. 2021, DOI 10.1029/2020WR028134 (TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED)
Basu et al. 2010, GRL, DOI 10.1029/2010GL045168 (VERIFIED)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The prescription (use static long-term/legacy parameterization rather than time-varying surplus) costs no additional degrees of freedom - it REPLACES existing columns rather than adding them, which is the right shape at n=19.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: YES - a static per-basin surplus or legacy term is aggregable at any pin, and removes the 68%-NaN problem the 2017-terminating gTREND product currently creates.

findings.claim: SUPPORTING BUT WEAK EVIDENCE THAT TILE DENSITY DRIVES BETWEEN-SITE NITRATE LEVEL IN IOWA SPECIFICALLY - REPORTED WITH ITS SAMPLE SIZE BECAUSE THE SAMPLE SIZE IS THE STORY. UNVERIFIED (Gorski & Zimmer 2021, HESS 25:1333, DOI 10.5194/hess-25-1333-2021, five nested watersheds in the Raccoon River basin, central Iowa): cumulative annual NO3 load regressed on drainage-infrastructure density gives R2 = 0.71 (stormflow) and 0.75 (baseflow), rising to 0.88 and 0.88 for spring (April-June), p < 0.05. Median NO3 was 9.23 +/- 3.09 mg/L at the most heavily drained site (1.11 km/km2) versus 6.96 +/- 2.51 mg/L at the least drained (0.37 km/km2). HARD CAVEAT: every R2 here is fitted to FIVE points (3 df), in-sample, no validation of any kind, and the five watersheds are NESTED (the same pseudoreplication problem that collapses this project's 85 sites to 19 families), so effective n < 5. An R2 of 0.88 on n=5 is not distinguishable from noise at conventional power. Treat as a hypothesis-generating direction, NOT an expected effect size. The same paper reports that stormflow nitrate is CHEMOSTATIC across all seasons with event-averaged c-Q slopes distributed narrowly around zero, and that tile density has 'no systematic effect on stormflow c-Q slopes' - if true, that is a further argument that knowing Q buys near-zero marginal information about C during exactly the storm periods when daily-max nitrate and the 10 mg/L flag are highest. NOTE A CONFLICT: this stormflow-chemostasis reading sits uneasily with the VERIFIED finding of b = +0.61 median at this project's own gauged sites and b > 0 at 32/32 UMRB sites. The verified enrichment result WINS. The plausible reconciliation is timescale and flow-regime partitioning (event-scale storm slopes vs whole-record daily slopes), but this must be flagged as unresolved rather than papered over.
findings.effectSize: annual load vs drainage density R2 = 0.71 (stormflow) / 0.75 (baseflow); spring-only 0.88 / 0.88, p<0.05; median NO3 spread 6.96 to 9.23 mg/L across the density gradient; annual export 2,222 +/- 371 to 4,216 +/- 768 kg N/km2/yr; drainage density range 0.37-1.11 km/km2
findings.splitProtocol: not-applicable - in-sample OLS, no holdout of any kind
findings.nBasins: 5, NESTED, so effective n < 5
sources: Gorski & Zimmer 2021, HESS 25:1333, DOI 10.5194/hess-25-1333-2021 (TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED)
findings.feasibilityAtN19: The finding's own n is 5 nested watersheds, which is BELOW this project's 19 families - so this is not a large-n result that fails to transfer downward; it is a small-n result that should not be over-trusted upward. It is directionally consistent with the n=32 UMRB recomputation, which is the stronger of the two.
findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: The predictor (drainage-infrastructure density) YES if a statewide line layer exists; the c-Q slopes NO.

findings.claim: AN EXPLICIT, DIRECTLY APPLICABLE NEGATIVE RESULT AGAINST ENGINEERING A PER-SITE C-Q SLOPE AS A FEATURE. UNVERIFIED (Gorski & Zimmer 2021, Sect. 3.5): C-Q slopes are unstable to a handful of days. In one watershed, two anomalous low-flow low-nitrate events in October 2017 shifted the fall bulk stormflow c-Q slope from 0.09 to 0.71 (7.9x) despite representing '<1% of annual flow and NO3 load'. In another, an anomalous ~3-month low-flow window changed the annual baseflow c-Q slope from 0.42 to 1.42 (3.4x). The authors conclude: 'The ability of a single anomalous period (whether real or due to sensor artifacts) to influence the overall characterization of a hydrologic system highlights the difficulty in representing nutrient export behavior based on a single parameter fit across several seasons and flow regimes.' Separately, 'Seasonal and annual c-Q slopes across all hydrologic regimes show only weak correlations with watershed area' - so log_basin_area, the one relevant static attribute this project already has, does not predict c-Q behaviour. FALSIFIABLE PREDICTION: fitting a per-site c-Q slope as an engineered feature on this project's 22 gauged sites would produce estimates whose leave-one-out variance exceeds their between-site spread, and it would not transfer to the 63 ungauged sites at all. A related VERIFIED point reinforces this: the UMRB recomputation found b is only weakly land-use controlled (%row crop R2 = 0.345, %agriculture 0.310, %tile 0.209, log10(area) 0.147), so b is not reliably predictable from static attributes either - meaning there is no route to a c-Q slope at an ungauged pin.
findings.effectSize: one anomalous period changed the annual baseflow c-Q slope 0.42 -> 1.42 (3.4x); two events comprising <1% of annual flow changed a seasonal stormflow slope 0.09 -> 0.71 (7.9x); c-Q slope vs watershed area: 'only weak correlations', no R2 given. b predictability from static attributes: R2 0.147-0.345 (unverified UMRB recomputation).

Recomputation from Marinos et al. 2020 HydroShare archive (TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED)

findings.worksAtUngaugedPin: NO, on two counts: c-Q slope requires paired C and Q at the target (a pin has neither), and it is not reliably predictable from the static attributes that ARE available at a pin.

findings.claim: A CHEAP SIDE-LEAD WORTH SEPARATING FROM THE MAIN VERDICT: the riparian signal this project already tested may have been measured at the wrong scale. UNVERIFIED (Gorski & Zimmer 2021): 'The baseflow NO3 load during the summer is most strongly correlated with the percentage of cropped area within 100 m of the stream (R2 = 0.94; p < 0.01)'. This project's existing riparian test used a 0-2 km bucket and yielded CLF +0.039 PR-AUC with REG worse - a 20x wider band that would dilute a 100 m signal by roughly its area ratio. Recomputing crop fraction in a 100 m (or 100-500 m) stream buffer uses the same 30 m CDL grid already in the pipeline plus NHDPlus flowlines the project already has via COMID: no new data acquisition, no gauge, purely static, deployment-compatible. CAVEATS: R2 = 0.94 is fitted on FIVE nested watersheds in-sample with no validation, so it is a direction not an expected effect size; and the relation was established for SUMMER BASEFLOW LOAD specifically - the LOW-concentration regime (baseflow was <=15% of annual load in every watershed) - not the spring stormflow regime that carried 37.5 +/- 11.5% of annual load and produces the maximum concentrations that drive violation flags. So the reported relation is for the wrong regime for this project's target, and only the buffer-WIDTH lesson transfers.
findings.effectSize: summer baseflow NO3 load vs % cropped area within 100 m of stream: R2 = 0.94, p < 0.01 (n=5 nested, in-sample). Baseflow <=15% of annual load; spring stormflow 37.5 +/- 11.5%.

datasets.name: AgTile-US (30 m tile-drained cropland, CONUS)
datasets.url: https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/AgTile-US/11825742 (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.11825742; direct file example https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/23079140; paper DOI 10.1038/s41597-020-00596-x, open access via Europe PMC PMC7406500)
datasets.years: Single static epoch, 2017 census basis (built from USDA NASS 2017 Census of Agriculture county tile acreage + gSSURGO drainage class + SRTM slope + NLCD 2016 crop mask). NO time dimension.
datasets.access: figshare bulk HTTP download, NO authentication, NO cost. Files: AgTile-US-TIFF.zip (125.8 MB), AgTile-US-NetCDF.zip (128.9 MB), AgTile-US.zip (185.2 MB), plus a metadata txt. Download confirmed live by ranged GET. NOTE: the paper's own Data Availability section cites figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.12668234, but that item contains only a metadata record (data.json, 275-byte CSV) - use item 11825742. A Google Earth Engine community mirror (ee.Image('projects/sat-io/open-datasets/agtile/AgTile-US')) is reported but COULD NOT BE VERIFIED; treat as unconfirmed.
datasets.license: CC BY 4.0; the article is a US government work not under US copyright protection.
datasets.coversMultiState: YES - full CONUS (65d20'W to 127d53'W, 22d51'N to 51d36'N). This is decisive: it covers the Minnesota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Missouri and Illinois portions of Iowa's multi-state basins, i.e. exactly where the project's current Iowa-clipped CDL/N-surplus inner join under-counts worst. No NaN/partial-coverage flag needed for any Iowa basin.
datasets.whyUseful: Closes the project brief's stated #1 data gap ('tile drainage density ... NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet' - this is factually incorrect). Tile density is the control the C-Q literature identifies as dominant for Iowa nitrate LEVEL: verified in Marinos et al. 2020 as 'a dominant control on C-Q dynamics'; an unverified recomputation of that paper's archive found %tile alone explains R2 = 0.575 of between-site variance in fraction-of-days >= 10 mg/L (n=32), which is literally this project's classification target and its weakest term. It is a static between-site geographic feature - the only feature family that has produced wins here - and it requires no discharge record and no local history.
datasets.howToIncorporate: FEATURE NAME: tile_fraction (and tile_fraction_of_cropland). AGGREGATION: reproject the 30 m binary raster to the project's basin-cell grid; for each NLDI-delineated basin compute the area-weighted mean of the binary layer over all basin cells, giving tile_area/basin_area. ALSO compute tile_area/cropland_area using the existing CDL crop mask as denominator - a naive basin-mean conflates 'not tiled' with 'not cropland', and the two ratios carry different meaning (loading-relevant vs management-intensity). ADD THE SINGLE BASIN-MEAN SCALAR FIRST (1 degree of freedom against ~19 effective units). Only if that wins under LOFO should it be expanded to the existing 3 distance buckets (tile_fraction_0_Xkm etc., aggregated exactly like the 8 CDL crop classes already are). USE AS A TIME-INVARIANT STATIC COLUMN ONLY - never broadcast per-day as a pseudo-temporal variable; that is what produced the -0.166 result with 2017 N-surplus. Note the situations differ: N surplus is a genuinely time-varying quantity frozen at one year, whereas tile extent is a legitimately near-static basin property, so a static encoding is correct here rather than a compromise. ABLATION DESIGN: test against a lat/lon-INCLUDED baseline, not a stripped one, and report fold-level CIs.
datasets.limitations: (1) The '86.03% accuracy' figure is POSITIVE-CLASS RECALL ONLY - all 16,000 ground-truth points are known-drained locations, and 86.03% + 13.97% omission error = 100% exactly. No confusion matrix, no true negatives, no commission error, no kappa. A map that over-painted tile everywhere would score ~100% under this validation, and basin-MEAN fraction is biased precisely by the unmeasured commission error. (2) Validation points come from 10 states, not CONUS-wide, with ~5,253 (33%) in Iowa alone, spatially clustered, so effective n is far below 16,000; and points were restricted to fallow croplands 'where the tile drainage signature is easily detectable', making the figures optimistic. (3) Partial calibration/validation reuse: the slope thresholds constraining the decision tree were extracted from the same point set later used for validation. (4) CENSUS-CONSTRAINED BY COUNTY: cells are accumulated until the county total matches the 2017 census, so county aggregates reproduce the census by construction (Iowa -0.04% is a calibration target, NOT skill) and the genuine added value is only sub-county allocation via gSSURGO drainage class and slope. Effective independent information is county-scale (99 Iowa counties), not 30 m, with step discontinuities at county boundaries. (5) Known systematic low bias: USDA census tile estimates carry ~19.8% average error and NLCD 2016 underestimates cropland by -18.15% nationally, so tile area is under-allocated unevenly - a ~20% multiplicative noise floor that caps achievable between-site gain at n=19. (6) REDUNDANCY RISK: tile fraction is spatially very smooth across Iowa (Des Moines Lobe vs Loess Hills/driftless SE), and lon and lat are already the #2/#3 permutation-importance features, so XGBoost may already have absorbed most of this signal. Read a null result as 'already captured by coordinates', not 'tile drainage does not matter'; a control arm aggregating gSSURGO drainage class and slope directly would separate the two. (7) Static 2017 snapshot over a 2008-2026 record: reliable for between-site RANK, not for absolute drained area in any given year - the authors note tile drainage 'greatly expanded since the late 1990s'.

datasets.name: Nakagaki & Wieczorek, Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012 (USGS data release)
datasets.resolution: 30 m raster; each cell stores estimated tile-drained area in SQUARE METRES, so per-cell tile fraction = value/900. CONTINUOUS, not binary - a meaningful advantage over AgTile-US for computing a basin-mean fraction.
datasets.years: Single static epoch, 2012 (2012 Census of Agriculture state-level tile acreage + NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland + STATSGO2 poorly/moderately drained soils)
datasets.access: Free public bulk download from USGS ScienceBase, no authentication
datasets.license: USGS data release - public domain, no license restriction
datasets.coversMultiState: PARTIALLY - 12 Midwest states (SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY). Covers all of Iowa AND the MN/SD/NE/MO/IL headwaters of Iowa's multi-state basins, so it handles the normal case. But it is NOT CONUS-wide: Marinos et al. had to set tile = NA for one Mississippi-mainstem site because the basin extended beyond the 12-state layer. Any basin reaching outside the 12 states needs an EXPLICIT NaN/partial-coverage flag rather than a silent inner join - the exact failure mode that currently corrupts the project's crop/N-surplus aggregation.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the tile layer used by Marinos et al. (2020), so it is the layer underlying the n=32 UMRB between-site tile-vs-exceedance result. Using the same layer makes that unverified R2 = 0.575 result directly comparable rather than approximately so. Its continuous per-cell area encoding avoids the binary-threshold information loss in AgTile-US.
datasets.howToIncorporate: FEATURE NAME: tile_fraction_nakagaki. AGGREGATION: for each basin cell take value/900 to get per-cell tile fraction, then area-weighted-mean over the basin (and per distance bucket). This is exactly the conversion in Marinos et al.'s archived Step3_Compile_LULC.R ('Tiled = Tiledmean/900'). Use as a CONTROL ARM against AgTile-US: if the two layers give materially different basin-mean fractions, that disagreement is itself a useful uncertainty estimate on the feature, and the between-site result should be reported against both.
datasets.limitations: TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED. The DOI, ScienceBase item ID, resolution, unit encoding, coverage list and construction inputs all come from an unverified claim and MUST be confirmed against the ScienceBase record before any effort is spent. Also: older vintage (2012 vs 2017); state-level rather than county-level census constraint, so within-state allocation carries more of the modeling burden; 12-state extent requires explicit partial-coverage handling.

datasets.name: NOAA National Water Model CONUS Retrospective v3.0
datasets.resolution: Per NHDPlus v2 reach - 2,776,734 CONUS reaches; hourly streamflow in m3/s (plus 3-hourly land-surface output). Sibling Zarr stores for gwout, lakeout, ldasout and forcing.
datasets.years: 1979-02-01T01:00Z through 2023-02-01T00:00Z (385,704 hourly steps, 44 years). v2.1 covers Feb 1979 - Dec 2020 in bucket noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-pds with a separate Zarr mirror noaa-nwm-retrospective-2-1-zarr-pds.
datasets.access: Public AWS S3 (us-east-1), ANONYMOUS - `aws s3 ls --no-sign-request` or plain HTTPS GET. No AWS account, no authentication, no cost. NetCDF and Zarr. NOTE: the v3.0 bucket is not CONUS-only (top-level prefixes Alaska/, CONUS/, Hawaii/, PR/) so all paths need the CONUS/ prefix, and v3.0 Zarr lives inside the same bucket at CONUS/zarr/, unlike v2.1's separate mirror.
datasets.license: 'Open Data. There are no restrictions on the use of this data.'
datasets.coversMultiState: YES - CONUS-wide, covers every reach in and around Iowa's multi-state basins.
datasets.whyUseful: It is one of very few candidate sources genuinely compatible with the shipped product: unlike observed discharge (present at 22 of 85 sites, ZERO of 61 IWQIS sites), NWM covers all CONUS reaches, so it works at an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history and no gauged upstream neighbour. THE JOIN IS VERIFIED AND TRIVIAL: chrtout feature_id metadata states verbatim 'NHDPlusv2 ComIDs within CONUS, arbitrary Reach IDs outside of CONUS' (cf_role: timeseries_id), and the project already stores an NHDPlus comid per basin while NLDI delineation returns one - a single integer key lookup, no fuzzy spatial matching, no route-link file needed. The store also ships per-reach gage_id (NHD Gage Event ID), latitude, longitude, elevation and Strahler order. HOWEVER, the evidence in this angle says its EXPECTED VALUE AGAINST THE BETWEEN-SITE DEFICIT IS LOW - see limitations. It is documented here because the operational facts are worth having recorded, not because the discharge hypothesis survived.
datasets.howToIncorporate: DO NOT ingest raw daily modeled discharge as a per-day feature. That is 160k rows of a temporal hydrologic covariate - the exact category that has failed seven consecutive times on this project - and at 19 independent basin families it would be indistinguishable from noise. INSTEAD derive STATIC PER-BASIN FLOW SIGNATURES from the 44-year record at the basin-outlet COMID, one scalar each: nwm_mean_specific_q (44-yr mean flow divided by draining_area, mm/yr), nwm_baseflow_index (Lyne-Hollick or Eckhardt separation on the 44-yr daily series, ratio of baseflow to total), nwm_rb_flashiness (Richards-Baker index: sum of absolute day-to-day flow changes divided by total flow), nwm_runoff_ratio (mean annual runoff depth divided by mean annual precipitation from the existing weather layer), and nwm_q10 / nwm_q90 (low- and high-flow percentiles normalized by mean flow). That is 5-6 static scalars per basin, which is ~19-unit-affordable, and it targets the between-site term where headroom actually lies. nwm_mean_specific_q also serves as the water-yield DENOMINATOR for the mass-balance normalizer feature described in the findings. SEQUENCING - do these first: (1) download the 22 MB feature_id coordinate array, compute floor(index/30000) for the project's 85 COMIDs and count distinct feature-chunks, which decides whether extraction is ~2 GB or ~190 GB; (2) at the 22 USGS-gauged sites compute per-site KGE and MONTHLY PBIAS of NWM against observed Q, with attention to April-June; (3) regress NWM-vs-observed percent bias on AgTile-US tile fraction across those 22 sites. The gage_id array lets step (2) run without contaminating LOFO folds. If step (2) shows large, site-varying, spatially structured bias, abandon the modeled-Q avenue rather than proceeding.
datasets.limitations: (1) THE CORE PROBLEM IS NOT NWM'S ACCURACY, IT IS THAT DISCHARGE OF ANY PROVENANCE APPEARS NOT TO CARRY BETWEEN-SITE NITRATE-LEVEL INFORMATION - an unverified recomputation with PERFECT measured co-located Q found R2 = 0.034 for between-site mean nitrate and delta-R2 = +0.001 over a crops+tile model (n=32). Modeled Q can only add error on top of that. (2) NO TILE-DRAINAGE REPRESENTATION, verified through NWM v3.1 by source inspection of NCAR/wrf_hydro_nwm_public v5.4.0 (no OPT_TDRN, no TILE_DRAIN/TDRAIN, only generic Noah-MP QDRAIN) - so NWM does not supply the known-missing Iowa control either, and its hydrology in tile-drained basins is pathway-MIS-PARTITIONED (adding tile drainage changes peaks +14%, baseflow +11%, surface runoff -7 to -29%, recharge -43 to -50%, while annual volume moves only +2.3%). Note the derived claim that this produces a 'systematic low bias scaling with tile density' is NOT supported: the calibrated configuration shows peak bias +5% HIGH and low flows overestimated (+50%), and the source paper never regresses bias against tile percentage - its gauge sets are pre-screened to tile fraction >=10%, truncating the needed covariate range. (3) MODEST GAUGED SKILL, PARTLY IN-SAMPLE: Towler et al. 2023 report Central-region median KGE 0.45 (n=1,450) with calibration periods OVERLAPPING the evaluation window, so that is an optimistic figure; skill at an ungauged tile-drained agricultural pin should be assumed worse, since NWM calibrated at 1,378 predominantly NATURAL-FLOW basins and regionalized elsewhere. Two mitigating notes: the 'poor plains performance' band names ND/SD/NE/KS/TX, all WEST of Iowa (Iowa is in the zone the paper calls 'more mixed'), and the Central shortfall is driven by correlation (r 0.71) and variability ratio (rSD 0.87) rather than volume bias (PBIAS +4.4%) - i.e. it is a TIMING deficit, on the axis where this project is already adequate. (4) POSSIBLE EAST-WEST BIAS STRUCTURE ACROSS IOWA (UNVERIFIED): NCRFC natural-flow median PBIAS -10.15% at 100-500 km2 vs MBRFC +4.46% to +11.02%, a 15-20 point swing - and lon/lat are the #2/#3 features, so a west-east artifact is the worst possible failure mode. Also unverified: +47.14% median PBIAS at 10-100 km2 NCRFC regulated basins (small headwaters are where a map pin most often lands), and spring underestimation in humid regions precisely during the April-June nitrate flush. (5) TRAIN/SERVE SKEW: the retrospective ends Jan 2023 but the nitrate record runs to 2026. The gap must be filled from the operational bucket noaa-nwm-pds, a DIFFERENT product with a different model version and drifting calibration, and the retrospective performs NO streamflow data assimilation while the operational model does. That is a feature-distribution shift INVISIBLE in LOFO CV and a real deployment risk requiring an explicit consistency check on the overlap period. (6) ACCESS COST (UNVERIFIED but directly measured): chunking is [672 time, 30000 feature_id], 3.94 MB per compressed streamflow chunk, 573 time-chunks for the full record - 2 GB best case to ~190 GB worst case for 85 scattered COMIDs. Plan chunk-aligned batched reads.

datasets.name: Gorski et al. (2024) USGS data and model release - static watershed attributes for 46 US agricultural nitrate sites
datasets.url: https://www.sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/661436d1d34e633466530330 (DOI 10.5066/P1N6P2QL; also on catalog.data.gov). Companion paper DOI 10.1029/2023WR036591 (Wiley full text returns HTTP 403 to automated fetching despite hybrid open access).
datasets.resolution: Per-watershed static attribute table for 46 basins, plus daily dynamic inputs
datasets.years: Not determined - the exact train/validation/test years could not be retrieved from the paywalled text; the release is the authoritative route to them
datasets.access: Free, public domain, no authentication, via USGS ScienceBase
datasets.coversMultiState: Not applicable - it is a per-basin attribute table for 46 midwestern and eastern US sites, several of which are in Iowa. It is not a raster to aggregate.
datasets.whyUseful: Not a feature source but a DESIGN source. It supplies a ready-made, curated list of static watershed attributes assembled specifically for agricultural nitrate prediction - anthropogenic hydrologic modification (including artificial/tile drainage proxies), N application, climate, groundwater, land use/land cover, physiography and SOILS. Soil and physiographic attributes were reported (unverified) as ranking alongside discharge as the strongest influences on nitrate model performance, and this project currently has NO soil attributes, NO drainage class, NO depth-to-water-table, NO slope and NO relief - static geography is carried by lat, lon and log_basin_area alone. The release is also the authoritative route to the exact split protocol and per-site metrics that could not be extracted from the paper.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Read the attribute manifest and use it as a SHOPPING LIST for basin-aggregable static rasters, not as data to ingest directly. Priority candidates it should surface, each computed as a basin-mean (and per distance bucket only if the basin-mean wins): soil hydraulic conductivity and drainage class (gSSURGO or POLARIS), depth to water table, mean slope and relief, and a glacial hydrogeologic terrane / landform class. The terrane class is worth a dedicated test: encode each basin's Iowa landform region (Des Moines Lobe, Iowan Surface, Southern Iron Clay, Loess Hills) as a categorical FEATURE and test whether it beats or complements the raw lat/lon features that currently rank #2 and #3 - if terrane wins, the between-site deficit is a missing-geology problem; if not, lat/lon is capturing something else.
datasets.limitations: TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED throughout (the DOI, ScienceBase item ID and attribute list all rest on unverified claims and should be confirmed before effort is spent). The associated modeling result is NOT transferable: median KGE 0.66 comes from 46 single-site LSTMs with observed daily discharge as a required input, every scheme trained on data FROM the sites being predicted, and no experiment withholding a site entirely - a temporal holdout at gauged sites, NOT comparable to this project's LOFO 0.820. Use the attribute list; do not use the architecture or the performance number. Their grouping strategy (5-8 groups over 46 sites) also does not scale down: at 19 families it gives ~2-4 families per group, below the point where a group-specific model can be fit.
