datasets.coversMultiState: NO. This is explicitly an Iowa agency product, so it will NOT cover the multi-state portions of the project's largest basins - reproducing exactly the existing crop/N-surplus under-counting bias for out-of-state area. This is a significant disadvantage relative to AgTile-US (CONUS) and Nakagaki (12 states).
datasets.whyUseful: Gorski & Zimmer (2021) computed drainage-infrastructure density from this layer and reported it as the strongest between-site control on annual nitrate load in the Raccoon River basin. As a LINE-density measure it is conceptually different from AgTile-US's AREA-fraction measure - it captures conveyance intensity rather than drained extent - so it is a genuinely independent second view of the same control, worth testing if the area-fraction feature underperforms.
datasets.howToIncorporate: FEATURE NAME: drainage_line_density. AGGREGATION: clip the line layer to each delineated basin, sum line length in km, divide by basin area in km2. Reference values from Gorski & Zimmer for sanity-checking: 1.11 km/km2 (heavily drained Upstream Sac City) to 0.37 km/km2 (least-drained Middle Redfield). Use ONLY as a secondary/control feature after AgTile-US tile_fraction, and only for basins fully within Iowa - basins extending out of state need an explicit partial-coverage flag, never a silent inner join.
datasets.limitations: TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED, and the weakest-specified dataset here. The source paper gives NO URL, NO layer name, NO vintage and NO statement of statewide completeness; all of this must be independently verified (or obtained by emailing Iowa DNR) before any claim of Iowa-wide coverage. Iowa-only extent reintroduces the multi-state truncation bias. The supporting effect sizes (R2 0.71-0.88) rest on FIVE NESTED watersheds fitted in-sample with no validation, so they are a direction, not an expected effect size.

datasets.name: Marinos, Van Meter & Basu (2020) C-Q analysis archive (HydroShare)
datasets.url: https://www.hydroshare.org/resource/d5676355cbd94b79a2e58f8089040a40/ (DOI 10.4211/hs.d5676355cbd94b79a2e58f8089040a40). Companion paper DOI 10.1029/2020GL087051 is CLOSED access (Unpaywall is_oa=false, zero OA locations, agupubs HTTP 402).
datasets.resolution: Per-site records for 33 UMRB sites (35 raw archived): USGS NWIS gauges in HUC 07 with in-situ optical nitrate sensors (parameter 99133) AND co-located instantaneous discharge (00060), >365 days of record. Includes the paper's R code (Step1_Grab_And_Munge_Data.R, Step3_Compile_LULC.R).
datasets.years: Not stated; each site has >365 days of high-frequency (5-15 min to daily-mean) nitrate sensor data
datasets.coversMultiState: Not applicable - it is a site-level analysis archive for the Upper Mississippi River Basin, not a raster. UMRB/HUC-07 includes many Iowa gauges.
datasets.whyUseful: This is the single most directly on-point dataset in the corpus: 33 UMRB sites (32 usable) with paired high-frequency nitrate and co-located discharge, in the project's own region and at the same order of sample size as its 19 independent basin families - so unlike CAMELS-scale evidence it is NOT infeasible here. It is the source of the recomputed between-site results that answer the research question: %tile alone R2 = 0.575 for exceedance-day fraction versus log10(mean specific discharge) R2 = 0.097 and delta-R2 = +0.001 when added to crops+tile. It also contains the paper's own methodological choices, notably that discharge is converted to SPECIFIC discharge (Q_cfs * 2.447 / Area_km2) before all C-Q fitting.
datasets.howToIncorporate: Not a feature source - a VALIDATION and PRIOR-SETTING source. Two uses: (1) re-run the between-site regressions independently to confirm or refute the unverified R2 = 0.575 (tile) vs R2 = 0.034 (specific discharge) contrast before committing to either the tile feature or the discharge feature; (2) use its site list as an external comparison set, since HUC-07 overlaps this project's own sites - which is also the CAVEAT below.
datasets.limitations: TIER 3 for all recomputed numbers - UNVERIFIED. Every recomputed R2 is an IN-SAMPLE cross-sectional fit of one static covariate against a site-level summary statistic, with NO held-out predictive score, so none of it is comparable to LOFO 0.820. The paper itself is closed-access, so its published b values, CVc/CVq figures, site count, drainage-area range and breakpoint parameters are NOT retrievable ('six orders of magnitude' is the only sourceable quantitative figure); the recomputation fits a single OLS log-log line on unweighted daily means whereas the paper fits a broken power law by maximum likelihood on flow-weighted daily concentrations, so the b values are comparable in sign and order but are NOT the paper's estimates. Its site set spans six orders of magnitude in area within one basin, so nested-catchment pseudoreplication in the CVc/CVq-vs-area regression is plausible and undetermined. MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT: the sites are HUC-07 USGS nitrate-sensor gauges, which may substantially OVERLAP this project's own training network - in which case this is a prior analysis of our own data, not independent corroboration. Check the site list against the project's 85 sites BEFORE citing any of it as external validation.

refuted.claim: Nitrate in agricultural catchments dilutes with discharge, so C = load / Q (a dilution mass balance) is the right functional form for a concentration feature or target.
refuted.refutation: Wrong sign. VERIFIED on this project's own data: median C-Q exponent b = +0.61 across the 20 usable gauged sites - strongly mobilizing/enriching. Corroborated (unverified) at 32/32 UMRB sites, b range +0.090 to +1.095, median +0.440, with not one site diluting on the daily-mean timescale; and (unverified) in 274 German catchments where 82.1% have b > 0 and only 5.8% show genuine dilution (b <= -0.1). Dilution is a real C-Q regime, but not this one.

refuted.claim: Basu et al. (2010) establish concentration ~ N-input-yield / specific-discharge as a validated between-site relation.
refuted.refutation: VERIFIED FALSE. The paper proposes the decomposition C_f = L_T/Q_T and asserts that 'the anthropogenic drivers (e.g., land-use; nutrient inputs) are reflected in C_f' - but it NEVER fits that relation. There is no regression of C_f on N input, N surplus, land use, or specific discharge, and NO between-catchment R2 appears anywhere in the paper. C_f is a per-catchment fitted slope requiring the site's OWN paired load and discharge record. It is a decomposition framework, not evidence.

refuted.claim: The Basu 2010 headline result (annual load vs annual discharge, R2 = 0.7 +/- 0.2) supports predicting nitrate from discharge.
refuted.refutation: Three verified scope violations. (a) It is an INTER-ANNUAL, WITHIN-CATCHMENT regression, each catchment fitted separately - not a between-catchment relation, so it is no evidence about the absolute level of an unseen basin. (b) The target is LOAD, which contains Q on both sides; the authors explicitly acknowledge the critique that this 'is a spurious correlation since discharge is a component of load calculation', and note linear L-Q fits reach R2 > 0.8 for b anywhere in (-0.4, 1.4) - a band including strong dilution AND strong mobilization, so a high L-Q R2 does not establish that concentration is flat. (c) The timescale is ANNUAL on catchments of 10^4-10^6 km2, roughly 10-30 points each. This project predicts DAILY-max concentration and daily threshold exceedance on far smaller basins.

refuted.claim: Iowa agricultural nitrate is chemostatic, so discharge carries little information about concentration and the fluid-dynamics angle can be killed on that basis.
refuted.refutation: The premise is wrong and the test built on it has a broken decision rule. VERIFIED: Basu et al. 2010 state that nutrient export in the MARB is NON-chemostatic at DAILY and MONTHLY timescales - chemostasis emerges only after annual aggregation, so it provides no support at this project's operative timescale. Marinos et al. show chemostasis WEAKENS with basin size across six orders of magnitude, and Iowa's monitored network sits at the larger, less chemostatic end. Thompson et al.'s own nitrate result is mean CVc/CVq = 0.70 (SD 0.49) in a paper with only 2 agricultural catchments. AND THE TEST WAS RUN: median CVc/CVq = 0.443 on this project's gauged sites - 'well below 1', which by the stated criterion would kill the angle - yet log Q explains a median 50.9% of within-site log-nitrate variance at those same sites with b = +0.61. CVc/CVq is low there because CVq is LARGE (median 1.4), not because C is insensitive to Q; it is a variance ratio, not a mutual-information measure. The angle should be down-weighted for the absence of a between-site Q-to-level relation, NOT for chemostasis.

refuted.claim: The chemostatic threshold is CVc/CVq < 0.3 (Thompson et al. 2011).
refuted.refutation: VERIFIED FALSE as stated. No published source uses 0.3 as a community threshold. The value is 0.17 + 2 SD (0.06) of GEOGENIC solutes at Thompson's own 31 subwatersheds (nested in 9 experimental sites, 0.1-22 km2) - a relative reference calibrated on that dataset. The thresholds actually used in the literature are 0.5 (following Thompson et al. 2011, as adopted by Musolff et al. 2017 and Ebeling et al. 2021) or 1.0 (Musolff et al. 2015, DOI 10.1016/j.advwatres.2015.09.026). Attribution should be to Thompson et al. 2011 AND Musolff et al. 2015, and whichever threshold is used must be stated. Also: 'chemodynamic' never appears in Thompson et al.; CVc/CVq = 1 is Godsey et al. 2009's pure-DILUTION null (C ~ 1/Q), not a chemodynamic label.

refuted.claim: Switching the modeling target from concentration to LOAD (C x Q), then back-deriving concentration as L/Q, is a route to between-site skill.
refuted.refutation: Refuted on the source literature's own admission plus the observed C-Q sign. Basu et al. explicitly acknowledge the L-Q correlation is 'spurious since discharge is a component of load calculation', and show linear L-Q fits reach R2 > 0.8 across b in (-0.4, 1.4) - so a load target manufactures a high R2 that is largely an artifact. Worse here: since b > 0 essentially everywhere, load scales as roughly Q^(1+b) with 1+b in 1.09-2.10, making a load target MORE discharge-dominated than a concentration target; and back-dividing by a MODELED Q at the deployment target would propagate NWM discharge error straight into the shipped concentration estimate. This changes the target definition for no gain and adds a new error channel.

refuted.claim: NWM retrospective streamflow carries a structural, spatially systematic LOW bias in Iowa whose magnitude scales with tile density, making modeled-Q error correlated with the exact between-site gradient the model must learn.
refuted.refutation: The premise (NWM has no tile-drainage scheme) is VERIFIED and holds through v3.1 by direct source inspection. The derived bias claim is NOT supported and is partly contradicted. (a) SIGN: in the calibrated configuration the source paper reports median event peak-flow bias +5% (HIGH), reduced to +0.57% with tile drainage, and low flows OVERESTIMATED (still +50% even with the scheme). (b) The +14%/+2.3%/+11% figures are MODEL-MINUS-MODEL sensitivities between calibrated parameter sets, not measured biases against observations; adding tile drainage without recalibration barely moves the level at all, and the -43 to -50% figure is GROUNDWATER RECHARGE, an internal flux absent from the streamflow product. (c) THE SCALING WAS NEVER TESTED and the design cannot test it: both gauge sets are pre-screened to tile fraction >= 10%, truncating the range of the exact covariate the claim requires, and no regression of error against tile fraction appears anywhere in the paper. The residual error is better described as pathway MIS-PARTITIONING plus regionalization-donor artifacts than as tile-scaled low bias - still bad for a between-site feature, but for a different reason and with unquantified magnitude.

refuted.claim: Towler et al. 2023 report NWM v2.1 Central-region median KGE 0.40 (vs 0.29 for NHM v1.0) under a temporal holdout, and their 'poor plains performance' finding implies NWM is specifically weak over Iowa.
refuted.refutation: Three verified corrections. (a) VALUES: Central median KGE is 0.45 for NWMv2.1 and 0.33 for NHMv1.0 (n = 1,450, Falcone 2011 aggregated ecoregions, not HUC2); 0.29 is the West/NHM figure. CONUS-wide NWMv2.1 median is 0.53. (b) PROTOCOL: it is NOT a temporal holdout - both models' calibration periods OVERLAP the evaluation window (NWMv2.1 calibrated WY2008-2013), which the authors flag explicitly, so 0.45 is partly in-sample and optimistic. (c) GEOGRAPHY: the poor-plains sentence names North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas and Texas - all WEST of Iowa. Iowa sits in the eastern portion the paper calls 'more mixed' (the original quote 'most mixed' is a misquote), and no HUC-07 or Iowa-specific figure exists in the paper. The Central shortfall is also driven by correlation (r 0.71) and variability ratio (rSD 0.87) rather than volume bias (PBIAS +4.4%) - a timing deficit, not a level deficit.

refuted.claim: The project brief's statement that tile drainage density has 'NO data source identified yet'.
refuted.refutation: Factually incorrect. AgTile-US (VERIFIED: 30 m, CONUS, static 2017, CC BY 4.0, unauthenticated figshare download confirmed live, Iowa validation 91.1% on 5,253 points) has been publicly available since 2020, published by the same first author as the NWM tile-drainage study. A second option, Nakagaki & Wieczorek's USGS 12-state continuous tile-area raster (UNVERIFIED), is also free and public domain. Correcting this is arguably the highest-value output of this entire research angle.

refuted.claim: Nitrogen surplus is the right between-site source term for predicting a basin's mean nitrate level.
refuted.refutation: Contradicted from two directions. UNVERIFIED (Ebeling et al. 2021, n=759): N surplus correlates with mean nitrate at only r = 0.39 (r2 ~ 0.15) and appears in the top six predictors of NEITHER the PLSR nor the RF model, while plain forest fraction alone explains 32% and agricultural fraction 29% - despite N surplus correlating strongly with agricultural land (r = 0.71). VERIFIED (Basu et al. 2010): annual flow-weighted concentration in the MARB stayed invariant despite a ~1.5x increase in nutrient inputs over three decades, and Baltic ~50% input-reduction efforts 'failed to show positive results', because export is 'transport- rather than supply-limited'. Together these suggest the gTREND surplus product may be the wrong VARIABLE, not merely the wrong vintage - independently explaining this project's -0.166 result from broadcasting 2017 surplus forward, and favouring land-cover fractions plus subsurface/tile attributes over an N-budget product.

refuted.claim: Pooling more catchments reliably improves nitrate prediction, as it does for streamflow in CAMELS.
refuted.refutation: UNVERIFIED but explicitly stated as a negative result in Gorski et al. (2024, n=46): a global pooled LSTM achieved median KGE 0.63 versus 0.66 for single-site models, 0.66 for 5 attribute clusters and 0.65 for 8 glacial-terrane groups. The authors conclude there is 'a threshold of dissimilarity beyond which more data does not improve the model' and note 'it is not clear that this is true for water quality constituents'. This cuts both ways for this project: it weakens the claim that n=19 families is fatal, and it weakens the claim that acquiring more sites would fix the between-site deficit.

uncovered: USGS SPARROW predicted mean-annual flow and nitrogen yield per reach - EXPLICITLY REQUESTED BY THE RESEARCH BRIEF AND ENTIRELY ABSENT FROM THE EVIDENCE. No claim, verified or unverified, mentions SPARROW. Its coverage, model vintage (Midwest/MRB regional SPARROW), reach-level output format, COMID join, access route, license, and - critically - whether its predicted mean-annual N YIELD per reach is skilful as a between-site covariate at an ungauged pin, are all unassessed. This is the single most conspicuous gap: SPARROW predicts exactly the between-site quantity this project lacks (a per-reach N delivery estimate), it is free and USGS-published, and it was named in the brief. It should be the first target of any follow-up research on this angle. NOTE A LIKELY COMPLICATION to check first: SPARROW is calibrated against observed loads at monitoring stations that probably include some of this project's own sites, so using SPARROW output as a feature risks target leakage into the LOFO folds.

GAGES-II - EXPLICITLY REQUESTED BY THE BRIEF AND ABSENT. It appears only in passing (Towler et al.'s 5,390 'cobalt gages' are described as GAGES-II derived). Its ~300 static basin characteristics per gauge - the standard US catchment-attribute compendium, and precisely the class of between-site static information this project is missing - are never evaluated. Coverage, variable list, whether attributes are computable for an ARBITRARY delineated basin (they are published per GAUGE, which may make them unusable at a map pin without recomputing from the underlying source rasters), access and license are all unassessed. The recomputability question is the decisive one and is unanswered.

Regionalizing streamflow from this project's own 22 gauged sites to the 63 ungauged ones - EXPLICITLY REQUESTED BY THE BRIEF AND COMPLETELY UNADDRESSED. No source in the corpus evaluates donor-basin transfer, area-ratio scaling, drainage-area-ratio regionalization, or regional regression of flow statistics at anything like n=22 donors. The relevant negative context is indirect: NWM's own regionalization (Gower's-distance from 49 donors to 939 HUC10 receivers) was never independently validated in its source paper, which suggests the difficulty is real but supplies no effect size. Given that measured specific discharge appears to carry near-zero between-site nitrate information anyway, this gap may be moot - but it was asked for and produced nothing.

The Damkohler number framing (Oldham, Basu) - NAMED AS A SEED IN THE BRIEF AND PRODUCED NOTHING. No source in the corpus discusses reaction-vs-transport timescale ratios, Damkohler numbers, or the associated framework for predicting when a catchment behaves chemostatically versus reactively. Since this is the main theoretical apparatus for predicting C-Q regime FROM catchment properties - i.e. exactly the ungauged-transfer problem - its absence is a substantive gap, not a cosmetic one.

Van Meter & Basu on legacy nitrogen and transit times - NAMED AS A SEED AND ESSENTIALLY UNCOVERED. Legacy N appears only as a mechanism invoked inside other claims (Basu 2010's transport-limitation argument). No primary legacy-N or transit-time source was retrieved, no quantitative legacy-N accumulation estimates for Iowa basins, and no assessment of whether a legacy-N proxy is computable at an arbitrary ungauged pin. This matters because multiple lines in this corpus converge on legacy N as the correct between-site state variable in place of contemporary surplus - the recommendation is well-motivated but its primary evidence base was never retrieved.

Godsey / Kirchner power-law C-Q as a PRIMARY source - NAMED AS A SEED, cited only second-hand. Godsey et al. 2009 appears once, inside a correction, as the origin of the CVc/CVq = 1 pure-dilution null. The primary power-law C-Q literature was never retrieved, so the canonical b-value distributions and their catchment-property controls are not independently established here.

AN OPERATIONAL SPEC FOR THE LONG-TERM RUNOFF / PRECIPITATION CLIMATOLOGY LAYER needed for the one surviving mass-balance prescription. The finding that site-mean concentration ~ (N source term) / (long-term mean annual runoff) is deployment-compatible and cheap, but NO verified dataset spec was obtained for the denominator. PRISM 30-year normals and Daymet are named in verifier corrections as plausible sources, with no resolution, coverage-years, URL, access mechanism, or license verified for either, and no assessment of whether a gridded RUNOFF (as opposed to precipitation) climatology with CONUS coverage exists in free form. Without this the normalizer feature cannot be built as specified. Note NWM v3.0's 44-year record could supply a modeled mean specific discharge instead - but that reintroduces exactly the modeled-Q error the angle otherwise avoids, so an observation-based climatology is preferable and its spec must be sourced.

NWM v3.0 SKILL SPECIFICALLY IN TILE-DRAINED MIDWEST AGRICULTURAL BASINS. This is the assessment the brief called essential ('this bias assessment is essential - modeled Q error could swamp the signal'), and it does not exist in the retrieved literature. Towler et al. aggregate to broad ecoregions with no Iowa or HUC-07 figure. Valayamkunnath et al. is NWM V2.0 and never regresses error against tile fraction. The Water 15:2319 per-RFC PBIAS figures are UNVERIFIED and contain no tile-drainage, soil-drainage-class, or relief-stratified evaluation at all. One researcher's web-search budget was exhausted before finding peer-reviewed regional validation. TREAT NWM IOWA SKILL AS AN OPEN QUESTION, NOT A GIVEN. Two concrete routes remain unexplored: the USGS ScienceBase NWM v2.1 daily benchmark dataset (reported at sciencebase.gov/catalog/item/62336af9d34ec9f19eeb48fd, UNVERIFIED), which reportedly publishes per-gauge NSE/KGE and would allow computing the Iowa-specific distribution directly; and the direct test at this project's own 22 gauged sites, which dominates further literature search.

WHETHER MODELED Q RETAINS THE INFORMATION THAT OBSERVED Q CARRIES. Every within-site C-Q result in this corpus uses OBSERVED discharge. No source evaluates whether a modeled discharge surrogate preserves that relationship. The concern is specific and unquantified: NWM Q at an Iowa basin is itself largely a deterministic function of the same weather forcing and basin geometry already in this project's feature set, so its MARGINAL information content over the existing 68 features may be far below what the observed-Q results suggest - possibly near zero even before model error is considered. No study in the corpus tests this, and it is cheaply testable at the 22 gauged sites.

THE PROJECT'S OWN UNUSED CO-LOCATED WATER CHEMISTRY, which is arguably a better fluid-dynamics proxy than modeled discharge and was not covered by any source. Specific conductance is present at 65 of 85 sites and is a well-known conservative-tracer proxy for flow-path partitioning and baseflow fraction; turbidity (61 sites) indexes surface-runoff contribution; water temperature (80 sites) carries groundwater-contribution signal. No retrieved source evaluates these as nitrate predictors. CRITICAL DEPLOYMENT CAVEAT that must be stated if this is pursued: these are SENSOR observations at monitored sites and are NOT available at an arbitrary ungauged map pin, so they could only serve as a research diagnostic (e.g. to establish what flow-path information WOULD be worth having, thereby guiding which static proxy to build) - never as a deployed feature.

RECONCILIATION OF A CONFLICT LEFT OPEN IN THE EVIDENCE. Gorski & Zimmer (2021, unverified) report stormflow nitrate as CHEMOSTATIC with event c-Q slopes narrowly around zero across all five Iowa watersheds, whereas the VERIFIED whole-record daily fits give b = +0.61 median at this project's own sites and b > 0 at 32/32 UMRB sites. The verified enrichment result wins on tier rules. The plausible reconciliation is a timescale/flow-regime distinction (event-scale storm slopes versus whole-record daily slopes, and stormflow versus baseflow partitioning), but this was not resolved by any source and should be flagged as open rather than assumed away - it bears directly on whether Q could matter during the specific storm windows that drive 10 mg/L exceedances.
